42858633.label: Purpose
42858633.text: To systematically review MRI-derived radiomic and artificial intelligence models predicting outcomes in men on or eligible for active surveillance (AS) for prostate cancer, and whether reported endpoints permit quantitative synthesis.

42858633.label: Method
42858633.text: Following PRISMA 2020, we searched PubMed, Scopus, Embase, and Web of Science (2000-September 2026). Two reviewers independently screened, extracted data, and assessed risk of bias (QUADAS-2, PROBAST) and methodological quality (METRICS). Three subgroups were defined: AS selection at diagnosis, baseline detection of clinically significant cancer, and progression during follow-up. Pooling was pre-specified for subgroups with at least four independent cohorts; endpoint equivalence was assessed.

42858633.label: Results
42858633.text: Seventeen studies across 12 unique cohorts were included. Seven publications derived from two cohorts; 12 independent cohort-level estimates (n = 2703) remained after overlap resolution. Nine publications (four independent cohorts) addressed progression (AUC 0.70 to 0.95), but progression was defined in five non-equivalent ways, from any grade-group increase to composite core-count criteria, precluding quantitative synthesis. Risk of bias was high or unclear in 16 of 17 studies; the median METRICS score was 32.3 % (range 18.9-52.3 %). No study reported external validation or calibration for progression.

42858633.label: Conclusions
42858633.text: Progression endpoints were heterogeneous and several were of limited clinical relevance. A core outcome set for AS (at least ISUP grade group ≥3 and/or unequivocal radiological progression), followed by multi-centre external validation with a head-to-head comparison against the PRECISE v2 (Prostate Cancer Radiological Estimation of Change in Sequential Evaluation) score, is the priority before clinical use can be considered.

42900033.label: Background
42900033.text: Perivascular adipose tissue (PVAT) density on coronary computed tomography angiography (CTA) reflects pericoronary inflammation, but measurements adjacent to existing plaques may be confounded by local inflammatory signaling from the plaque itself-a form of reverse causation. Whether systematically comparing patient-level PVAT aggregation approaches (including measurements restricted to plaque-free segments) can identify a more robust inflammatory biomarker has not been evaluated.

42900033.label: Objectives
42900033.text: The authors aimed to compare the predictive performance of 4 patient-level PVAT aggregation approaches for coronary plaque progression.

42900033.label: Methods
42900033.text: From the PARADIGM serial coronary CTA registry, 412 patients with baseline coronary plaque who underwent serial coronary CTA at identical tube voltages were included (mean age: 61.1 ± 9.3 years; 61.7% male; mean interval: 3.2 ± 1.2 years). Four patient-level PVAT measures were compared: proximal right coronary artery (pRCA), whole-coronary, plaque-free, and plaque PVAT. Multivariable regression models were constructed for annualized plaque volume (PV) progression with adjustment for clinical risk factors and imaging covariates.

42900033.label: Results
42900033.text: Annualized increases in pRCA PVAT (β = 0.804; P = 0.033), whole-coronary PVAT (β = 1.142; P = 0.022), and plaque-free PVAT (β = 1.419; P = 0.007) were each independently associated with total PV progression, whereas plaque PVAT did not reach significance (β = 0.755; P = 0.083). For noncalcified PV progression, plaque-free PVAT was the only significant measure (β = 1.086; P = 0.026). None of the 4 baseline PVAT measures were significantly associated with plaque progression (all P > 0.50). Pairwise comparisons revealed no significant differences among the 4 measures.

42900033.label: Conclusions
42900033.text: Changes in pRCA, whole-coronary, and plaque-free PVAT were each independently associated with total PV progression. For noncalcified PV progression, plaque-free PVAT change was the only significant measure.

42914183.text: Although 18F-FDG PET is commonly used in the differential diagnosis of cognitive decline, synaptic vesicle glycoprotein 2A PET may offer a more direct assessment of synaptic integrity and address limitations associated with 18F-FDG, such as sensitivity to sensory stimuli and glycemic variations. In this study, a head-to-head comparison of 18F-SynVesT-1 and 18F-FDG was performed for differentiating causes of cognitive decline in a tertiary clinical setting. Methods: Patients with cognitive decline referred for 18F-FDG PET were recruited to undergo 18F-SynVesT-1 PET/MRI (49 ± 26 d after 18F-FDG PET). Diagnosis was determined by routine clinical follow-up (median, 11 mo) and classified as Alzheimer disease (AD), frontotemporal degeneration (FTD), dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB), other neurodegenerative disorders (ONDs), or nonneurodegenerative disorders (NoNDs). Volume-wise and voxelwise semiquantitative analyses were performed using tracer-specific healthy volunteers. Diagnostic accuracy for both tracers was evaluated through logistic regression and by consensus from 3 readers. Noninferiority was defined by an area-under-the-curve margin (ΔAUC) of -0.10 within a 95% CI, using the clinical follow-up diagnosis as the gold standard. Results: Ninety-four patients were included: 44 with AD, 12 with FTD, 4 with DLB, 5 with ONDs, and 29 with NoNDs. Volume-wise and voxelwise analyses showed that, in patients with AD and DLB, reductions in the temporoparietal and precuneus/posterior cingulate were less pronounced with 18F-SynVesT-1 PET than with 18F-FDG PET (e.g., posterior cingulate in AD, -10% vs. -20%). In FTD, the most impacted areas showed greater variability, typically affecting the anterior temporal and frontal cortices, depending on the FTD subtype. Visual assessment showed lower sensitivity for AD with 18F-SynVesT-1 PET than with 18F-FDG PET (0.57 vs. 0.73) with equal specificity (0.76), whereas quantitative analysis yielded a lower area under the curve (0.71 vs. 0.81; ΔAUC, -0.10; 95% CI, -0.21 to 0.01). For FTD, 18F-SynVesT-1 visual classification yielded similar sensitivity and specificity (0.58 and 0.90) compared with 18F-FDG (0.50 and 0.93) but a lower quantitative area under the curve (0.64 vs. 0.76; ΔAUC, -0.12; 95% CI, -0.27 to 0.04). Conclusion: 18F-SynVesT-1 PET enabled accurate classification of disease-specific patterns of cognitive decline. Although classification performance for FTD was similar to that of 18F-FDG PET, the lower effect size in neocortical binding resulted in lower sensitivity for AD. Larger study samples are needed to formally evaluate tracer noninferiority in this clinical context for all subgroups.

42918883.label: Objective
42918883.text: The presence of extra-pancreatic nerve plexus invasion (EPNI) in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is known to correlate with aggressive disease, however, it is unknown whether specific pathways or morphologies carry different prognostic implications. This study evaluates whether distinct CT-defined patterns of EPNI predict mortality in PDAC.

42918883.label: Materials and methods
42918883.text: This retrospective, single-center study included 89 patients with pathologically confirmed PDAC who underwent preoperative pancreatic protocol multidetector CT (MDCT) followed by surgical resection. Patients were identified from an institutional database and required available preoperative CT and histopathology. Two blinded, experienced radiologists reviewed MDCT images to assess EPNI, which was categorized by anatomic pathway and morphologic pattern. Overall survival was compared between EPNI-positive and EPNI-negative groups and among EPNI subtypes using log-rank testing, with stratification by tumor stage. Cox proportional hazards models adjusted for age, sex, and surgical margin were performed.

42918883.label: Results
42918883.text: A total of 89 patients (M/F: 54/35), median age: 66 years (IQR, 60-70 years), were evaluated. CT evidence of EPNI was present in 65 patients (73%) and was associated with decreased overall survival (p < 0.001). This association remained significant in Stage I tumors (p < 0.001). PPC2 pathway involvement (p < 0.001) and mass-with-stranding morphology (p < 0.001) were each associated with reduced overall survival. PPC2 (p = 0.003) and mass-with-stranding (p < 0.001) remained significant in stage I tumors.

42918883.label: Conclusion
42918883.text: Preoperative CT detection of EPNI, especially PPC2 pathway involvement and mass-with-stranding morphology, identifies high-risk PDAC patients.

42918883.label: Key points
42918883.text: Question Extra pancreatic nerve plexus invasion in pancreatic adenocarcinoma is associated with aggressive disease, but the prognostic significance of specific pathways or morphologies remains unknown. Findings Plexus pancreaticus capitalis 2 involvement and mass-with-stranding morphology in EPNI of pancreatic adenocarcinoma are associated with decreased overall survival. Clinical relevance Identifying high-risk EPNI features on CT may facilitate early prognostic stratification and inform surgical and neoadjuvant treatment planning in pancreatic adenocarcinoma.

43007083.text: Background Glandular tissue component (GTC) at breast US is associated with breast cancer risk, but recurrence risk remains unclear. Purpose To evaluate the association between GTC assessed at preoperative breast US and recurrence risk in invasive breast cancer across two tertiary institutions in Korea and China. Materials and Methods This retrospective longitudinal study included consecutive women with invasive breast cancer who underwent surgery between January 2013 and December 2018 in Korea and between January 2013 and December 2019 in China. GTC was qualitatively classified as low (minimal or mild) or high (moderate or marked) on preoperative bilateral US images. GTC was prospectively assessed during routine clinical care at institution A (Korea) and retrospectively assessed using archived images at institution B (China). Competing-risk multivariable Fine-Gray models evaluated GTC as the independent variable for recurrence, with adjustment for clinicopathologic variables. Results Mean age was 52.4 years ± 10.8 (SD) at institution A (n = 5167) and 49.2 years ± 10.1 at institution B (n = 3719). Median interval from surgery to recurrence diagnosis or last follow-up was 6.8 years (IQR, 5.42-8.41 years) at institution A and 8.0 years (IQR, 6.38-9.60 years) at institution B. Ipsilateral or contralateral breast cancer occurred in 145 (2.8%) and 85 patients (2.3%) at institutions A and B, respectively, while regional or distant recurrence occurred in 233 (4.5%) and 520 (14.0%). In multivariable analyses, high GTC was independently associated with increased risk of ipsilateral or contralateral breast cancer at institution A (subdistribution hazard ratio [HR], 1.93; P < .001) and institution B (HR, 2.02; P = .002). There was no evidence of an association between GTC and regional or distant recurrence at either institution A (HR, 0.89; P = .46) or institution B (HR, 1.20; P = .06). Conclusion High GTC at preoperative breast US was independently associated with an increased risk of ipsilateral or contralateral breast cancer after invasive breast cancer treatment, consistently across both institutions.

43019233.text: An 81-year-old man presented with new-onset right lumbodorsal pain, four years after radical nephrectomy for right renal cell carcinoma. 18F-FDG PET/CT revealed a high-density focus with intense radioactivity in the midline of the abdomen, corresponding to a urachal calculus. This case highlights the importance of recognizing urachal calculus as a potential false-positive finding in 18F-FDG PET/CT.

43050083.label: Objective
43050083.text: This study compares the diagnostic performance of US and 3-T MRIin diagnosing placenta accreta spectrum (PAS) disorder using final histopathological and surgical findings and explores the benefit of using a combined MRI and US approach to diagnose PAS.

43050083.label: Materials and methods
43050083.text: We retrospectively reviewed electronic medical records of all patients undergoing 3-T MRIplacenta at our institution between January 2020 and November 2023. The gold standard for PAS outcome was histopathology, and where unavailable, we referred to the operative notes. Patients without surgical or histopathologic data, and non-diagnostic MRI studies were excluded. Sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value (PPV), negative predictive value (NPV), confidence intervals, and p-values were generated for MRI, US, and combined MRI + US to detect PAS with subgroup analysis for placenta accreta/increta and percreta.

43050083.label: Results
43050083.text: Eighty-eight patients met the inclusion criteria. The sensitivity and specificity of MRI for all PAS was 100.0% and 80.0% (p < 0.001), compared to US 89.5% and 62.0% (p < 0.001), and combined MRI + US 100.0% and 56.0% (p < 0.001), respectively. For diagnosing placenta percreta, MRI had a sensitivity and specificity of 83.3% and 94.3% (p < 0.001), compared to US 55.6% and 94.3% (p < 0.001) and combined MRI + US 83.3% and 92.9% (p < 0.001).

43050083.label: Conclusion
43050083.text: Both US and 3-T MRIdemonstrated strong diagnostic performances for detecting PAS, with 3-T MRIdemonstrating stronger performance in this selective cohort, and not further improved by including US data. The continued use of US, MRI and clinical data for evaluating PAS disorder treatment options is recommended.

43050083.label: Key points
43050083.text: Question No dedicated study has evaluated the diagnostic performance of 3-T MRIor the combined use of MRI with US in PAS. Findings 3-T MRIdemonstrates high sensitivity and specificity for diagnosing PAS. The combined MRI and US assessment does not further improve diagnostic performance for PAS. Critical relevance statement 3-T MRImay be particularly useful as an adjunct in selected high-risk patients, equivocal ultrasound cases, or cases requiring assessment of myoinvasive disease and multidisciplinary surgical planning.

43076683.text: Background Mild hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy (HIE) comprises approximately 30%-50% of neonatal encephalopathy cases, yet neurodevelopmental outcomes remain difficult to predict using clinical assessment alone. Purpose To develop and externally test a diffusion kurtosis imaging (DKI)-based machine learning model for predicting 24-month neurodevelopmental outcomes in neonates with mild HIE. Materials and Methods This prospective four-hospital study consecutively enrolled neonates from November 2019 through November 2023, with 24-month follow-up completed in November 2025. The primary outcome was adverse neurodevelopment at 24 months, defined as any Bayley Scales of Infant and Toddler Development, third edition, composite score below 85; cerebral palsy; or epilepsy requiring ongoing treatment. Clinical-only, imaging-only, and combined clinical-imaging models were developed from 49 DKI parameters and seven clinical variables. Model discrimination was assessed with the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), and curves were compared with paired DeLong tests and false discovery rate adjustment. Results Overall, 740 neonates were included (mean gestational age, 38.3 weeks ± 1.3 [SD]; 404 [54.6%] female). Adverse outcomes occurred in 182 of 510 development cohort participants (35.7%) and 80 of 230 external test set participants (34.8%). In the external test set, the combined model achieved an AUC of 0.92 (95% CI: 0.89, 0.95), with a sensitivity of 86% (69 of 80) and specificity of 85.3% (128 of 150). It exceeded the clinical-only model (AUC, 0.85; false discovery rate-adjusted P = .004) and imaging-only model (AUC, 0.86; false discovery rate-adjusted P = .005). Prespecified risk stratification yielded a negative predictive value of 100% (61 of 61) for low-risk infants and a positive predictive value of 88% (38 of 43) for high-risk infants. Conclusion In neonates with mild HIE, a combined clinical and DKI model demonstrated higher discrimination for predicting 24-month neurodevelopmental outcomes than did clinical-only or imaging-only models.

43084083.label: Purpose
43084083.text: This study aimed to assess the potential of abbreviated dynamic [18F]FDG PET imaging using a long axial field-of-view (LAFOV) scanner for non-invasive characterization of tumor subtypes and prediction of programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) status in treatment-naïve patients with non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC).

43084083.label: Methods
43084083.text: 51 treatment-naïve patients with histologically confirmed NSCLC (34 adenocarcinomas [LUAD], 17 squamous cell carcinomas [LUSC]) underwent a 20-min dynamic [18F]FDG PET/CT acquisition starting 45-min post-injection on an LAFOV system. Parametric images of net influx rate (Ki) and distribution volume (DV) were reconstructed using a direct Patlak approach with patient-specific scaled population-based input functions. PD-L1 tumor proportion score was determined from one histopathologically sampled lesion per patient.

43084083.label: Results
43084083.text: PD-L1 positive lesions demonstrated higher SUVmax (16.9 ± 9.6 vs. 11.6 ± 5.7; p = 0.04), Kimax (0.077 ± 0.04 vs. 0.054 ± 0.02; p = 0.03), and DVmax (428.7 ± 253.5 vs. 278.7 ± 145.2; p = 0.02) than PD-L1 negative lesions. LUSC lesions showed higher SUVmax (18.7 ± 8.5 vs. 12.9 ± 8.2; p = 0.008) and Kimax (0.08 ± 0.02 vs. 0.06 ± 0.04; p = 0.02) than LUAD lesions, whereas DVmax did not differ (p = 0.69). In the histopathology-matched LUAD analysis, apparent/optimism-corrected AUCs were 0.74/0.70 for SUVmax/Kimax, 0.71/0.67 for Kimax/DVmax, and 0.75/0.71 for SUVmax/SUVpeak, without evidence of superior discrimination by any model.

43084083.label: Conclusion
43084083.text: PD-L1 prediction using both static and kinetic [18F]FDG PET parameters was feasible in NSCLC, with comparable performance between SUV- and parametric-based metrics, without evidence of superior discrimination by any model. These preliminary findings require validation in larger independent cohorts. Abbreviated dynamic LAFOV PET/CT enables whole-body assessment of tumor glucose kinetics in a clinically practical protocol.

43084433.text: Diagnosis and management of lower genitourinary trauma presents substantial challenges to the complex anatomy and functional diversity of the affected organs. Imaging plays a critical role in accurately assessing the injury location and severity, guiding clinical decisions, and improving patient outcomes. US, CT, and conventional urethrography and cystography are commonly used for the initial assessment of patients with lower genitourinary trauma. MRI, with its superior soft-tissue contrast resolution and direct multiplanar imaging capability, is invaluable in selected cases of lower genitourinary trauma. MRI has a complementary role in diagnosis of acute penile fractures and testicular injuries when US findings are inconclusive, as MRI effectively delineates the tunica albuginea of the corpora of the penis as well as the testicles. Disruption of the tunica albuginea is an indication for immediate surgical repair. Traumatic urethral injuries can lead to strictures and disruptions, which often necessitate delayed reconstructive surgery. MRI has an adjunctive role in conventional urethrography and provides detailed anatomic information about the urethra and periurethral structures such as urethral stumps, urethral gap length, periurethral fibrosis, displacement of the prostate and rectum, fistulas, false channels, fractures and avulsions of the corporal bodies, and fluid collections such as hematoma, urinoma, and abscess. Bladder rupture with surrounding fluid collection can be identified at MRI, although confirmatory CT or conventional cystography may be necessary. Furthermore, MRI with and without intravenous contrast material is helpful for diagnosis of suspected partial segmental thrombosis of the corpus cavernosum.
